title: Creative testing lab
summary: How many creatives to test, how long and how much to spend on each, and how to read the results without fooling yourself. You leave with exact starting rules for killing, holding, iterating and scaling, and a weekly sprint you can run from next Monday.

lessons.title: What you are testing: the testing ladder
objectives: By the end you can name the five levels of a creative test: concept, angle, hook, format and iteration.
You can explain why big changes are tested before small ones, and put a test on the right rung of the ladder.
You can name ads so any teammate can read what a test changed.

steps.h: Testing is how you buy knowledge
steps.p: Most creatives lose. In Module 3 you saw an example month where 20 ideas produced one winner worth scaling. That is normal. The money you spend on tests is tuition. Spend it on clear questions and it buys answers. Spend it on muddled tests and it buys nothing you can reuse.
steps.more: Example: two buyers each spend $300 on creative tests in a week. Buyer A launches six random ads that differ in angle, hook, format and lander all at once. One does well, but she cannot say why, so she cannot repeat it. Buyer B tests four concepts with everything else fixed. One wins, and he knows it was the idea, so next week he makes three more ads on that idea. Same money, very different value.

d.b: A test is a paid question
d.s: Ask one clear question per test

steps.say: Let's start with an honest truth: most creatives lose. In Module three you saw an example month where twenty ideas produced one winner worth scaling. That's normal. The money you spend on tests is tuition. Spend it on clear questions and it buys answers. Spend it on muddled tests and it buys nothing you can reuse. For example, a buyer who changes everything at once may find a winner but can't say why. A buyer who tests one thing knows exactly what to repeat. A test is a paid question.

steps.p: A creative has layers. Each layer is a different thing to test, and each answers a different question. Knowing which layer you are changing is the first rule of testing. Concept, angle, hook and format come from Module 3; here we put them in order.
d: Concept|the whole idea: one angle, one format, one core message
Iteration|one small change to a proven ad
steps.say: A creative has layers, and each layer is a different thing to test. Look at the five cards. Concept, the whole idea: one angle, one format, one core message. Angle, why the viewer should care. Hook, the first one to three seconds. Format, like a talking head, a demo, a static image or a carousel. And iteration, one small change to a proven ad. Knowing which layer you're changing is the first rule of testing.

steps.h: One offer, five levels of change
steps.p: Example: an education offer that teaches beginners to use a demo trading account. Each row is a test at a different level. Notice how the size of the change shrinks as you go down. Bigger changes can move results more, and also fail more often.

rows: New captions or a shorter cut

steps.say: Here's one example offer, an education offer that teaches beginners to use a demo trading account, tested at each level. A concept test compares a teacher's story with an app demo, the biggest change. An angle test compares learn safely with understand risk. A hook test compares a question opener with an on-screen fact. A format test compares a talking head with a static image. And an iteration tries new captions or a shorter cut, the smallest change. Notice the size shrinks as you go down. Bigger changes can move results more, and also fail more often.

steps.p: Example from one illustrative account: the gap between the best and worst cost per registration at each level of testing. Concept tests produced a 3x gap; iterations only 1.15x. Your numbers will differ, but the pattern is common: big levers move results more.
steps.more: Read the bars as the ratio between the worst and best variant in a typical round at that level. Example: in a concept round the worst concept cost $15 per registration and the best $5, a 3x gap. In an iteration round the worst cut cost $5.75 and the best $5, a 1.15x gap. These are illustrative figures, not industry statistics. The lesson is about order: find a good idea first, then polish it.
steps.say: These bars come from one illustrative account. They show the gap between the best and worst cost per registration at each level. Concept tests produced a three times gap. Angle, about two times. Hook, one point six. Format, one point four. And iterations only about one point one five. These aren't industry statistics, and your numbers will differ. But the pattern is common: big levers move results more. So find a good idea first, then polish it.

steps.p: Climb from the biggest lever to the smallest. Find a concept that works, then test hooks on it, then port it to other formats, then keep it fresh with iterations. When a winner fades, you climb back to the top and look for the next concept.
steps.say: This is the testing ladder. Follow it from the top. Concepts, to find the idea. Hooks, to open it better. Formats, to reach more places. Iterations, to keep it fresh. And then back to new concepts. Why loop back? Because when a winner fades, you climb back to the top and look for the next concept.

steps.p: Example: target cost per registration is $5. Your concept costs $8. You test hooks and the best one improves it by 15%. The result is $6.80, still over target. Polishing a weak idea rarely rescues it. A new concept round found one at $4.50.
steps.more: Check: $8.00 × 0.85 = $6.80. To reach $5 from $8 you need a 37.5% improvement, because ($8 − $5) ÷ $8 = 0.375. Hook tests on a proven idea often give gains of 10% to 25% in our experience, which is a rough guide, not a rule. That is great on a $5 concept, taking it to about $4, and not enough on an $8 one. This is why you climb the ladder in order.
steps.say: Here's why order saves money, as an example. Your target cost per registration is five dollars. Your concept costs eight. You test hooks, and the best one improves it by fifteen percent. Look at the equation: eight dollars times zero point eight five gives six dollars eighty, still over target. Polishing a weak idea rarely rescues it. To get from eight to five you'd need a thirty seven and a half percent improvement. A new concept round found one at four dollars fifty.

steps.p: Every test changes one layer and freezes everything else. Write the question before you build anything. If you cannot say in one sentence what the test will teach you, it is not ready.
steps.say: Every test changes one layer and freezes everything else. Look at the table. A concept test changes the whole idea and keeps audience, lander and event fixed, asking which idea sells. A hook test changes the first three seconds and asks which opening stops people. A format test asks whether it works elsewhere. An iteration changes one element and asks whether this version is better. Write the question before you build anything. If you can't say in one sentence what the test will teach you, it isn't ready.

steps.h: Where each test lives in the account
steps.p: A simple setup: new concepts and iterations are tested in a separate test campaign. Proven winners move to a main campaign that holds the scaling budget. Every result, win or lose, goes into the creative log, which feeds the next brief.
steps.say: Look at this map of where each test lives. A creative brief launches into a separate test campaign. An ad that passes the rules becomes a proven winner and graduates to the main campaign, which holds the scaling budget. The winner also gets new hook iterations, which go back into the test campaign. And every result, win or lose, goes into the creative log, which feeds the next brief.

steps.h: Name ads so the test reads itself
steps.p: A naming rule turns your ad list into a readable report. Put the concept, angle, hook, format and version in every ad name. Then anyone can sort the list and see which layer won, without opening each ad. Field names change; check the current Ads Manager.
steps.more: Keep names short and the same order every time. Use the same IDs in your creative log, your tracker's sub IDs and your network sub IDs, so a row in the network report can be matched to an exact ad. Avoid spaces and special characters in names you pass into tracking links.

steps.p: These mistakes waste most beginner test budgets. Each one makes the result impossible to read or puts effort on the wrong rung of the ladder.

items: Polishing hooks on an unproven idea
Changing concept and hook at once
No names, so no one knows what won

items: Big levers first, small ones later

And no names, so no one knows what won. On the right, the fixes: prove the concept first. One layer per test. Big levers first, small ones later. And use the naming rule on every ad.

steps.p: Move a concept from the concept rung to hook testing only when it passes the final read: spent at least 3x target CPA, cost per result at or under 0.8x target, with 3 or more conversions on network data. Starting rule; adapt it with your own results.

steps.say: Here's a starting rule for when to climb. Move a concept up to hook testing only when it passes the final read. It has spent at least three times target C P A, cost per acquisition. The concept spent seventy five dollars for four F T Ds, eighteen seventy five each. It passes. Adapt this rule with your own results.

steps.p: Testing does not make a dishonest ad acceptable. Never test fake testimonials, actors posing as customers, invented results or fake scarcity. If AI made or changed a face or voice, disclose it where rules require. Use real people, with consent, and disclose paid partnerships.

takeaways: A creative has five testable layers: concept, angle, hook, format and iteration.
Climb the ladder from big levers to small ones; polishing a weak concept rarely saves it.
One layer changes per test, and the ad name records which one.

quiz.q: Your new concept costs $9 per registration against a $5 target. What should you test next?
options: Five new hooks on this concept
New concepts, because polishing is unlikely to close a 44% gap
A bigger budget on the same ad
quiz.why: You would need about a 44% improvement to reach $5. Hook tests rarely deliver that, so a new concept round is the better use of money.

quiz.q: Which change is an iteration?
options: Swapping a teacher's story for an app demo
Changing the angle from learning to risk
Adding captions to a proven video, nothing else
quiz.why: An iteration changes one small element of a proven ad. The others change the concept, the angle or the offer.

quiz.q: You change the hook and the format in the same test, and results improve. What do you know?
options: Something improved, but not which change caused it
quiz.why: Two changes at once make the result impossible to attribute. Test one layer at a time.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a naming rule?
options: It lets anyone read what each ad tested and match it to network data
It makes the platform favour your ad
It is required by every network
quiz.why: Names that record concept, angle, hook, format and version make results sortable and traceable to tracker and network sub IDs.

quiz.q: A concept spent 3x target CPA with 4 conversions at 0.75x target on network data. Under the starting rule, what next?
options: Kill it, four is too few
Start a brand new concept round and forget it
quiz.why: It passed the final read: at least 3x spend, 3 or more conversions and cost at or under 0.8x target. It earns hook tests.

lessons.title: How many creatives and how to structure the test
objectives: By the end you can work out how many concepts your budget can test fairly.
You can compare three test structures and choose one for your budget.
You can build a clean test campaign step by step.

steps.h: Too many ads starve, too few miss
steps.p: Every extra ad splits the same money into smaller pieces. Starve each ad and none gets enough data to judge, so you pick winners by luck. Test too few and you may never find a winner at all. The count is a budget decision, not a creative one.
steps.say: Every extra ad splits the same money into smaller pieces. Starve each ad, and none gets enough data to judge, so you end up picking winners by luck. Test too few, and you may never find a winner at all. That's why the count is a budget decision, not a creative one. The budget sets the count, not your list of ideas.

steps.p: Starting rule: each concept needs about 3x your target CPA to reach a final call. Divide your test budget by that amount. Example: $300 test budget and a $25 target cost per FTD gives four concepts.
steps.more: Check: 3 × $25 = $75 per concept. $300 ÷ $75 = 4. Then apply the range rule: test at least 3 and at most 6 concepts per round. Fewer than 3 and you learn too little per round. More than 6 on a small budget and each concept gets too little money. If the formula gives fewer than 3, the next slide shows what to do.
steps.say: Here's the concept count formula, a starting rule. Each concept needs about three times your target C P A, cost per acquisition, to reach a final call. Divide your test budget by that amount. Look at the example on screen: a three hundred dollar test budget, and a twenty five dollar target cost per F T D, first-time deposit. Three times twenty five is seventy five per concept. Three hundred divided by seventy five gives four concepts. Then apply the range rule: at least three, at most six concepts per round.

steps.h: How many concepts for your budget
steps.p: Example with a $25 target cost per FTD. Starting rule: 3 to 6 concepts per round, each with about 3x target CPA. If the budget cannot fund 3, judge on a cheaper event first, as lesson 3 shows. Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical.
steps.say: This table uses a twenty five dollar target cost per F T D. Four hundred and fifty dollars funds six concepts, the upper limit. Three hundred funds four, which is comfortable. Two hundred and twenty five funds three, the minimum. And with one hundred and fifty, you can only give three concepts fifty dollars each, so judge on registrations first, as lesson three shows. This is a rough guide, and it varies by geo and vertical.

steps.p: In a concept test the idea changes and nothing else does: same audience, same placements, same conversion event, same lander, same budget per concept. In an iteration test only one element of the ad changes. Anything else that moves becomes a hidden second variable.

steps.h: Three ways to structure a test
steps.p: There is no single correct structure. Each trades fairness against speed and cost. Module 3 introduced these; here is how to choose between them and set them up.
d: One ad set, many ads|fast and cheap; the platform decides who gets spend
One ad per ad set|fairer spend; more ad sets to manage
Platform test tool|cleanest split; usually needs more budget and time
steps.say: There's no single correct structure. Each one trades fairness against speed and cost. Look at the cards. One ad set with many ads is fast and cheap, but the platform decides who gets the spend. One ad per ad set gives fairer spend, with more ad sets to manage. And the platform's own test tool gives the cleanest split, but usually needs more budget and time.

steps.p: Choose by budget and by how much you need a fair answer. With small budgets, speed and simplicity matter. With larger budgets, fairness is worth paying for, because a wrong winner costs more when you scale it.
steps.say: Here they are side by side. Many ads in one ad set: low spend fairness, cheapest and fastest, best under fifty dollars a day. One ad per ad set: high fairness, medium cost, best at fifty dollars a day and up. The platform test tool: highest fairness, slowest and most budget, best for big, close decisions. With small budgets, speed and simplicity matter. With larger budgets, fairness is worth paying for, because a wrong winner costs more when you scale it.

steps.p: Example: five concepts in one ad set with $100 of spend. The platform gave $62 to concept A within two days. Concepts D and E got $5 and $3. You learned a lot about A and almost nothing about D and E. They are unproven, not losers.
steps.more: Check: $62 + $21 + $9 + $5 + $3 = $100. The platform moves spend to ads that look promising early, which is good for results and bad for fair tests. If your target CPA is $25, A spent about 2.5x target, but E spent only 0.12x. Starting rule: an ad that spent less than 1x target CPA has not been tested. If its early signals were fine, re-test it in its own ad set next round.
steps.say: This is what uneven spend looks like, as an example. Five concepts in one ad set, one hundred dollars of spend. Look at the bars. The platform gave sixty two dollars to concept A within two days. B got twenty one, C got nine. And D and E got just five and three dollars. You learned a lot about A and almost nothing about D and E. They're unproven, not losers. The starting rule: an ad that spent less than one times target C P A hasn't been tested.

steps.p: This is the recommended starting structure once you can afford it. One test campaign holds one ad set per concept. Every ad set has the same audience, event and daily budget. Results go to the log, and winners graduate to the main campaign.

A concept that looks great after eight dollars may be average. That's why you decide your spend checkpoints before launch, and then read only at those points. Stopping early is the costliest mistake.

steps.p: Starting rules, measured per creative in multiples of your target CPA. They match the kill, hold and scale rules used across this school. Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical; adapt with your own data.
steps.more: Example with a $25 target cost per FTD: early read at $12.50, first kill read at $50, final call at $75. Between 0.8x and 1.5x target at the final call, hold: keep the ad running at the same budget and add iterations beside it. These rules match the kill-or-scale lab used in this school, so the lab's verdicts will agree with them.

rows: Kill only if CTR is under half your norm
Scale if CPA 0.8x or less, 3+ conversions

steps.say: These are the starting spend rules, measured per creative in multiples of your target C P A, cost per acquisition. The early read is at half of target with two thousand plus impressions, and you only kill if C T R, click-through rate, is under half your norm. The first kill read is at two times target: kill if there are zero conversions. The final call is at three times target: kill if C P A is over one point five times target, scale if it's zero point eight or less with three or more conversions. Then a lag check two days after you stop.

steps.h: Minimum data before reading each metric
steps.p: Each metric needs its own minimum. Read a metric before it has enough data and you are reading noise. Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical.
steps.say: Each metric needs its own minimum data before you read it. Hook rate, after one thousand impressions: do people stop? Link C T R, after two thousand impressions and twenty clicks: do they click? C P C, cost per click, after fifty link clicks. Cost per registration, after five registrations or two times its target. And cost per F T D, first-time deposit, after three times target C P A plus two days. Read a metric too early and you're reading noise. This is a rough guide, and it varies by geo and vertical.

steps.p: Spend checkpoints tell you how much. Time windows tell you how long. Use both: a creative is ready for its final call only when it has reached the spend and the time.
d: 3 full days|the minimum before any final call
5 to 7 days|ideal, so weekdays and a weekend are included
+2 days|for late deposits to arrive by postback
72 hours|no edits after launch, they reset learning
steps.say: Spend checkpoints tell you how much. Time windows tell you how long. Look at the cards. Three full days is the minimum before any final call. Five to seven days is ideal, so weekdays and a weekend are included. Add two more days for late deposits to arrive by postback. And no edits for seventy two hours after launch, because edits reset learning. A creative is ready for its final call only when it has reached both the spend and the time.

steps.p: Example: cumulative cost per registration for two concepts over 7 days. After day 1, concept B looked nearly four times worse. By day 7, B was the cheaper one. Judging on day 1 would have killed the better concept.
steps.more: Why it happens: on day 1 each concept had only one or two registrations. One extra registration on day 1 halves the cost; one missing doubles it. As counts grow, each new result moves the average less, and the lines settle. Module 9 covers the statistics in depth; for now, remember that early averages are built on tiny counts.
steps.say: Look at these two lines, an example of cumulative cost per registration over seven days. After day one, concept B looked nearly four times worse than A, nine dollars against two fifty. But follow the lines. By day seven, B was the cheaper one, at about four thirty against five twenty. Judging on day one would have killed the better concept. On day one each concept had only one or two registrations, so one extra result swings the average a lot.

steps.h: Early signals versus the real KPI
steps.p: Read the funnel top down. Early signals arrive fast and in volume. The real KPI, usually cost per FTD or cost per paid event, arrives late and in small numbers. Each step is a filter, not a verdict.
d: Cost per FTD: does it pay?
steps.say: Read the funnel from the top down. Hook rate: do they stop? C T R: do they click? C P C: is the click affordable? Then cost per registration. And finally cost per F T D: does it pay? Early signals arrive fast and in volume. The real K P I, your key performance indicator, usually cost per F T D, arrives late and in small numbers. Each step is a filter, not a verdict.

steps.h: Use early signals to kill, never to scale
steps.p: A creative that nobody stops for will not make money, so weak early signals are a fair reason to cut. A creative with great early signals can still attract curious clickers who never deposit. Scale only on the paid event.

a.title: Early signals may
items: Kill very weak ads at 0.5x target
Rank ads for a second look

steps.say: Here's the key principle. On the left, early signals may kill very weak ads at half of target, rank ads for a second look, diagnose hook or body problems, and flag broken links fast. On the right, early signals may not pick the winner, justify scaling, overrule network F T D data, or replace the final call. Why? A creative nobody stops for won't make money. But a creative with great early signals can still attract curious clickers who never deposit. Scale only on the paid event.

steps.h: Price the whole test before launch
steps.p: Example: target cost per FTD $25, four concepts, 3x target each for the final call. The test costs $300. At $60 a day across four ad sets, it runs five days, then two more days for late deposits before the final read.
steps.more: Check: $25 × 3 = $75 per concept. $75 × 4 = $300. $300 ÷ $60 a day = 5 days, which also meets the 5 to 7 day window. Concepts that hit a kill rule early stop spending, so the real total is often lower. Set this $300 aside before you launch. If you cannot afford it, test fewer concepts or judge on a cheaper event.
steps.say: Price the whole test before you launch. In this example, target cost per F T D is twenty five dollars, there are four concepts, and each gets three times target for the final call. Look at the equation: twenty five, times three, times four concepts, equals three hundred dollars. At sixty dollars a day across four ad sets, it runs five days, then two more days for late deposits before the final read. Set that money aside first. If you can't afford it, test fewer concepts or judge on a cheaper event.

steps.p: Example funnel for one concept at $75, using rates from an illustrative Kenyan education offer. Even at the full 3x budget, a concept performing on target produces only about 3 FTDs. That is enough to spot clear winners and losers, not to split close calls.
steps.more: Check: $75 ÷ $5 × 1,000 = 15,000 impressions. 15,000 × 1.0% = 150 clicks, so CPC = $75 ÷ 150 = $0.50. 150 × 10% = 15 registrations, $5 each. 15 × 20% = 3 FTDs, $25 each, exactly on target. If a concept is close to another, say $23 versus $27, run a second confirming round before you trust the gap.
steps.say: So what does seventy five dollars buy one concept? This example uses rates from an illustrative Kenyan education offer. At a five dollar C P M, cost per thousand impressions, that's fifteen thousand impressions. At one percent C T R, one hundred and fifty clicks. Ten percent register, so fifteen registrations. And twenty percent of those deposit, so three F T Ds. Even at the full budget, a concept on target produces only about three F T Ds. Enough to spot clear winners and losers, not to split close calls.

steps.p: Your turn. You test 4 concepts, each needs 3x a $25 target CPA, and you want the test done in 5 days. Enter 12 as conversions wanted (4 concepts × 3 target CPAs). What daily budget does the whole test need?
steps.more: Answer: 12 × $25 = $300, and $300 ÷ 5 days = $60 a day, which is $15 per concept ad set. If your account can only spend $30 a day, either run 2 concepts at a time over 10 days or switch to a cheaper judging event, as the next slide shows.

d.task: 4 concepts × 3x a $25 target = 12 target CPAs over 5 days. What is the daily budget for the whole test?

steps.say: Your turn, in the lab. You're testing four concepts. Each needs three times a twenty five dollar target C P A, and you want the test done in five days. Enter twelve as conversions wanted, because that's four concepts times three target C P As. Your job is to find the daily budget the whole test needs. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: When FTDs are too expensive to test on
steps.p: If 3x target CPA per concept is more than you can afford, judge the first round on registrations. Set a registration target from your FTD target, screen concepts on it, then confirm the survivors on FTDs. Starting rule; adapt it.

d.text: Example: target $25 per FTD and 20% of registrations deposit, so target per registration = $25 × 20% = $5. Final call on registrations at 3x = $15 per concept. Survivors get a second round judged on FTDs.

steps.say: What if three times target C P A per concept is more than you can afford? Then judge the first round on registrations. Here's the example. Target is twenty five dollars per F T D, and twenty percent of registrations deposit, so your target per registration is twenty five times twenty percent, five dollars. Your final call on registrations, at three times, is fifteen dollars per concept. Survivors then get a second round, judged on F T Ds. It's a starting rule, so adapt it.

steps.p: Concept C3 has run 3 days and spent $52 against a $25 target cost per FTD. The network shows 0 FTDs and you have checked that the postback works. Make the call using the starting rules.
steps.more: Answer: kill. $52 ÷ $25 = 2.08x target CPA with 0 conversions, which passes the first kill line of 2x. You checked the plumbing first, so the zero is real. Pause it, log the reason and the lesson, and let the other concepts finish.

d.task: C3: $52 spent, 0 FTDs on network data, target $25, 3 days. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Another lab, this time a decision. Concept C three has run three days and spent fifty two dollars, against a twenty five dollar target cost per F T D. The network shows zero F T Ds, and you've already checked that the postback works. Use the starting rules to decide: kill, hold or scale. Think about which spend checkpoint it has reached. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: These mistakes either kill good concepts too early or keep bad ones too long. Both cost money; the first one also costs you the winner you never found.

a.title: Mistake
items: Reading FTDs the night the test ends
Letting a loser run to 5x hoping

steps.say: These mistakes either kill good concepts too early or keep bad ones too long. On the left: judging on day one. Editing ads mid-test. Reading F T Ds the night the test ends. Letting a loser run to five times target, hoping. On the right, the fixes: read only at checkpoints. No edits for seventy two hours. Wait two days for late postbacks. And kill at the written line. Both errors cost money, and the first one also costs you the winner you never found.

steps.p: Platforms need some conversions before delivery settles, and big edits can restart learning. The exact thresholds change and we are not certain of current figures; check Meta's Help Center. A small test budget is never a reason to run claims or offers that are not approved.

d.text: Trading and gambling ads usually need platform authorization and must follow local law. Check both before you run any test, however small.

The exact thresholds change, and we're not certain of current figures, so check Meta's Help Center. And remember, a small test budget is never a reason to run claims or offers that aren't approved. steps.p: Use this list on the day of the final call. If any line is a no, wait or plan a confirming round rather than guessing.
d: Each creative reached 3x target spend or hit a kill line
At least 3 full days ran, ideally 5 to 7
steps.say: Use this list on the day of the final call. Did each creative reach three times target spend, or hit a kill line? Did at least three full days run, ideally five to seven? Have two days passed for late F T Ds? Does network data match the tracker? And was nothing edited mid-test? If any line is a no, wait, or plan a confirming round, rather than guessing.

takeaways: Checkpoints per creative: early read at 0.5x target, kill on zero at 2x, final call at 3x.
Each metric has its own minimum: about 1,000 impressions for hook rate, 2,000 and 20 clicks for CTR.
Run at least 3 full days, ideally 5 to 7, and wait 2 more days for late FTDs.
Early signals may kill weak ads but never justify scaling.
lessons.action: Write your checkpoint sheet for your next test: target CPA, the dollar amount of each checkpoint (0.5x, 2x, 3x), the minimum days, the lag day and the total test budget.

glossary.def: A spend level, set before launch, at which you read results and may make a decision.
A fast, high-volume metric such as hook rate, CTR or CPC that hints at performance but is not the result.
A second read of deposit data a couple of days after a test stops, so late FTDs are counted.
The conversion you use to make the test decision, such as registration in round one and FTD in round two.

quiz.q: Target cost per FTD is $40. At what spend per creative is the first kill read for zero FTDs?
quiz.why: The first kill read is at 2x target CPA: 2 × $40 = $80.

quiz.q: After 600 impressions, ad A has a 1.9% CTR and ad B 0.8%. What should you do?
options: Wait; CTR needs about 2,000 impressions and 20 clicks
quiz.why: 600 impressions is too few to read CTR reliably. Wait until the minimum is reached.

quiz.q: A concept has a superb hook rate and CTR, but after 3x target spend its cost per FTD is 1.7x target. What now?
options: Scale it, the early signals are great
Kill it; early signals never overrule the paid event
quiz.why: CPA above 1.5x target at the final call is a kill. Early signals can kill, but they cannot rescue or scale.

quiz.q: Target $30 per FTD, 25% of registrations deposit. What is the target cost per registration?
quiz.why: Target per registration = $30 × 25% = $7.50.

quiz.q: The test ends Friday evening. When should you make the final FTD call?
options: Sunday or Monday, after late postbacks arrive
quiz.why: Deposits often arrive days after the click. Wait about 2 days so the slower concepts are counted fairly.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn how long to run a test and how much to spend before you judge it. You'll set spend checkpoints in multiples of target C P A, and learn to use early signals to kill weak ads, never to pick winners.
lessons.say_outro: So, decide your checkpoints before launch, read only at those points, wait for late deposits, and use early signals to kill, never to scale. Your task: write your checkpoint sheet for your next test, with target C P A, the dollar amount at half, two and three times target, the minimum days, the lag day and the total test budget. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Reading results without fooling yourself
objectives: By the end you can name four ways a creative test lies: noise, delivery bias, tracking gaps and time effects.
You can compare metrics against rough thresholds and, better, against your own account medians.
You can confirm a winner with network data and a second round before scaling.

steps.h: The numbers want to tell you a story
steps.p: After a test you will want a winner. That wish is dangerous. A false winner gets the scaling budget, and scaling a lucky ad buys you its average result at a bigger size. Example: $500 a week into a false winner at 1.5x target CPA loses money every day it runs.

d.b: Want the truth, not a winner
d.s: A false winner costs more than no winner

steps.say: After a test, you'll want a winner. That wish is dangerous. A false winner gets the scaling budget, and scaling a lucky ad buys you its average result at a bigger size. For example, putting five hundred dollars a week into a false winner running at one and a half times target C P A, cost per acquisition, loses money every day it runs. So want the truth, not a winner. A false winner costs more than no winner.

steps.p: Before you trust any result, ask which of these four might explain it. Usually one does. Module 9 goes deeper on noise; here we focus on what matters for creatives.
d: Delivery bias|the platform feeds early leaders
Tracking gaps|platform and network numbers differ
steps.say: Before you trust any result, ask which of these four might explain it. Usually one does. Noise: small counts swing by chance. Delivery bias: the platform feeds early leaders. Tracking gaps: platform and network numbers differ. And time effects: weekends, paydays and late deposits. Module nine goes deeper on noise. Here we focus on what matters for creatives.

steps.p: Example: five ads in one ad set. Ad A got slightly better early numbers, so the platform gave it more spend, which gave it more data, which earned it even more spend. By day 7 it had three quarters of the budget. That is efficient delivery, not proof that A is best.
steps.say: Look at how delivery bias snowballs, in this example. Five ads in one ad set. Ad A got slightly better early numbers, so the platform gave it more spend. That gave it more data, which earned it even more spend. Follow the lines: A starts at thirty percent of spend, and by day seven it has about three quarters of the budget, while the other four ads shrink. That's efficient delivery, not proof that A is best.

steps.p: Starting rule: any ad that spent less than 1x target CPA is unproven. Do not log it as a loser. If its hook rate and CTR were near your norm, re-test it in its own ad set next round with an equal budget.

d.text: Example: target $25. Ad D spent $9 with a hook rate of 27% against your 25% median. Unproven. It goes into next week's round as its own ad set at $15 a day.

steps.say: Here's a starting rule: starved is not lost. Any ad that spent less than one times target C P A is unproven, so don't log it as a loser. In the example, target is twenty five dollars, and ad D spent just nine dollars, with a hook rate of twenty seven percent against your twenty five percent median. It's unproven. If its hook rate and C T R, click-through rate, were near your norm, re-test it next round in its own ad set, with an equal budget.

steps.p: Rough guide, varies by geo, vertical, placement and format. Use these only until you have your own data. After 10 or more tests, compare every creative against your own account medians instead; they are far more useful.
steps.more: Hook rate is 3-second plays ÷ impressions; hold rate is ThruPlays ÷ 3-second plays (see Module 3). These are starting points from typical paid-social campaigns, not published statistics, and they can be far off for your geo or format. Static images have no hook rate. CTR on cheap, broad African placements can look high while deposits stay low. Build a simple median for each metric from your last 10 tests and replace this table with your own. Only cost per paid event decides winners.
steps.say: These are rough thresholds for weak, OK and strong, for hook rate, hold rate, link C T R, and cost per registration and per F T D, first-time deposit, compared with target. They're a rough guide, and they vary by geo, vertical, placement and format. They're not published statistics. Use them only until you have your own data. After ten or more tests, compare every creative against your own account medians instead. They're far more useful. And remember, only cost per paid event decides winners.

steps.h: Worked read: four concepts after the test
steps.p: Example: target $25 per FTD, each concept funded to $75, FTDs from network data after the 2-day lag. Apply the starting rules row by row before you look at anything else.
steps.more: Check: A $75 ÷ 5 = $15, and $15 ÷ $25 = 0.6x with 5 FTDs, which passes the scale line of 0.8x with 3 or more. B $75 ÷ 2 = $37.50 = 1.5x, which is not over the 1.5x kill line, so hold. C hit $50, 2x target, with 0 FTDs, so it was paused there. D $75 ÷ 3 = $25 = 1.0x, inside the hold band. Total spend: $75 + $75 + $50 + $75 = $275.
steps.say: Here's a worked read of four concepts. Target is twenty five dollars per F T D, each concept funded to seventy five, with F T Ds from network data after the two-day lag. A: five F T Ds, fifteen dollars each, zero point six times target, a winner to confirm, then scale. B: two F T Ds, thirty seven fifty, one point five times, so hold and add iterations. C: zero F T Ds at fifty dollars, killed at two times. D: three F T Ds at twenty five, one times target, hold. Apply the rules row by row before anything else.

steps.p: Use the starting rules on concept D: $75 spent over 5 days, 3 FTDs on network data, target $25 per FTD. Choose kill, hold or scale.
steps.more: Answer: hold. Cost per FTD is $75 ÷ 3 = $25, exactly 1.0x target. It is not cheap enough to scale (0.8x or less) and not expensive enough to kill (over 1.5x). Keep its budget the same and test iterations beside it.

d.task: Concept D: $75 spent, 3 FTDs, target $25, 5 days. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Now it's your turn. Use the starting rules on concept D. It spent seventy five dollars over five days, with three F T Ds on network data, and the target is twenty five dollars per F T D. Work out its cost per F T D, compare it with the scale and kill lines, and choose kill, hold or scale. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Starting rule for calling one creative better than another: the leader's cost per result is at least 30% lower, the leader has 5 or more conversions, and the gap held for at least 3 days. Example: A at $15 versus D at $25.
steps.more: If the gap is smaller than 30%, or the leader has fewer than 5 conversions, call it a tie and run a confirming round. Example: $23 versus $27 with 3 FTDs each is a 15% gap on tiny counts. That could easily flip next week. A tie is a fine result: keep both and test something with a bigger difference.
steps.say: When can you call one creative better than another? Here's the starting rule. The leader's cost per result is at least thirty percent lower. The leader has five or more conversions. And the gap held for at least three days. Look at the example: A at fifteen dollars against D at twenty five. Twenty five minus fifteen, divided by twenty five, is forty percent cheaper, with five F T Ds over three plus days. Likely real. If the gap is smaller, call it a tie and run a confirming round.

steps.p: The ad platform reports what it thinks happened. The network reports what the advertiser counted and will pay for. Make your final call on network numbers, matched to each ad by the sub IDs in your links.
steps.say: Look at this map. The ad sends a click with a sub I D to the lander, then to the offer sign-up, which the network counts. The network fires a postback for each F T D, matched by sub I D in your tracker, which feeds your test sheet as the network truth. Separately, the platform report gives its own view. The platform reports what it thinks happened. The network reports what the advertiser counted and will pay for. Make your final call on network numbers.

steps.h: Reconcile one test in a sheet
steps.p: Put platform and network numbers side by side for every ad. Small differences are normal; platforms may model some conversions and count by their own attribution window. Large gaps mean check tracking before deciding anything.
steps.more: Rough rule of thumb: if network registrations are within about 20% of the platform's, the tracking is probably fine. A, B and C are within that range. D shows 30 against 11, which suggests a broken link, a lander bug, or registrations landing under a different sub ID. In this example the fix was a typo in D's sub ID; after correcting it the network showed 27 registrations and the same 3 FTDs.

blocks.value: D: platform 30 vs network 11. Gap too big. Check the sub ID and postback before reading D.

steps.say: Put platform and network numbers side by side for every ad. Look at the table. A, B and C are close: small differences are normal, because platforms may model some conversions and use their own attribution window. But look at D: platform thirty, network eleven. That gap is too big. Check the sub I D and the postback before reading D. In this example, the cause was a typo in D's sub I D. Large gaps mean check tracking before deciding anything.

steps.p: These are the stories buyers tell themselves after a test. They feel like insight but they are wishes. Notice them, name them out loud and let the written rule make the decision instead.
d: Favourite creative|you made it, so you protect it
Story after the fact|inventing why it won once you see numbers
Peeking and switching|changing the judging metric to suit a favourite
Averages hide|one ad set blended into a good total
steps.say: These are the stories buyers tell themselves after a test. Favourite creative: you made it, so you protect it. Story after the fact: inventing why it won once you see numbers. Peeking and switching: changing the judging metric to suit a favourite. And averages hide: one ad set blended into a good total. They feel like insight, but they're wishes. Name them out loud, and let the written rule make the decision.

steps.p: A first-round winner is a candidate. Before it gets real money, confirm it once in a fresh setting. This costs a few days and protects you from scaling luck.
d: Duplicate into a fresh ad set
Run 3 days at the same budget
CPA still at or under target?
steps.say: A first-round winner is a candidate. Before it gets real money, confirm it once in a fresh setting. Follow the flow. Winner on network data. Duplicate it into a fresh ad set. Run three days at the same budget. Check: is C P A still at or under target? Then graduate it to the main campaign. This costs a few days, and protects you from scaling luck.

steps.h: A misleading win is not a win
steps.p: If an ad wins on CTR because the hook over-promises, it is not a winner. Watch the comments: "this is fake" or "scam" means trust is breaking, and complaints can hurt account health. Never treat a policy warning as a cost of doing business.

d.text: Trading and gambling ads usually need platform authorization and must follow local law. Check both before you run any test, however small.

steps.say: If an ad wins on C T R because the hook over-promises, it isn't a winner. Watch the comments. When people write this is fake, or scam, trust is breaking, and complaints can hurt account health. Never treat a policy warning as a cost of doing business. And trading and gambling ads usually need platform authorization and must follow local law. Check both before you run any test, however small.

steps.p: Run this before you write a single decision into your log. It takes about ten minutes and catches most false winners before they get a scaling budget they have not earned.
d: Each ad reached its checkpoint or a kill line
Network data reconciled with the platform
Starved ads marked unproven, not lost
Winner confirmed in a fresh ad set
steps.say: Run this checklist before you write a single decision into your log. Each ad reached its checkpoint or a kill line. Network data reconciled with the platform. Starved ads marked unproven, not lost. The gap rule passed: thirty percent or more, five or more conversions, three or more days. Comments checked for trust problems. And the winner confirmed in a fresh ad set. It takes about ten minutes, and catches most false winners.

takeaways: Four things make tests lie: noise, delivery bias, tracking gaps and time effects.
Rough thresholds help at first; your own account medians are better.
Call a winner only when it is 30% or more cheaper, with 5+ conversions, held 3+ days, on network data.
Confirm every winner in a fresh ad set before it gets scaling budget.

glossary.def: The platform's habit of giving more spend to ads that look good early, which makes in-ad-set tests uneven.
The middle value of a metric across your own recent tests, used as your personal benchmark.
To compare platform and network numbers for the same ads and explain any large gap before deciding.
A short re-test of a winner in a fresh ad set to check the result was not luck.
A starting rule for calling a winner: 30% or more cheaper, 5 or more conversions, and the gap held for 3 or more days.

quiz.q: Ad A received 74% of an ad set's spend by day 7. What does that prove?
options: The platform favoured A early; the others may be unproven
quiz.why: Delivery bias snowballs spend to early leaders. It is efficient delivery, not a fair comparison.

quiz.q: Ad X: $15 per FTD with 5 FTDs. Ad Y: $18 with 4 FTDs, over 4 days. Under the gap rule, what is the call?
options: Tie; the gap is under 30%, so run a confirming round
quiz.why: ($18 − $15) ÷ $18 is about 17%, under the 30% gap rule. Treat it as a tie.

quiz.q: Platform shows 30 registrations for an ad; the network shows 11. What first?
options: Check sub IDs, links and postbacks before deciding
Scale it, the platform likes it
quiz.why: A gap that large usually means a tracking or link problem. Fix the plumbing before you judge the creative.

quiz.q: After 15 tests, your median link CTR is 2.1% while the rough table says strong is over 1.5%. A new ad gets 1.6%. How do you read it?
options: Below your own norm, so look closer
The table is wrong, ignore CTR
quiz.why: Your own median is the better benchmark. 1.6% is below your usual 2.1%, so the ad is weaker than your typical creative on clicks.

quiz.q: Your first-round winner shows $15 per FTD. What should happen before it gets scaling budget?
options: Move it to a new geo
Confirm it in a fresh ad set for about 3 days
quiz.why: A confirming round checks the win was not luck or delivery bias before real money goes in.

lessons.title: Iterating winners and killing losers
objectives: By the end you can apply exact starting rules to kill, hold, iterate and scale creatives.
You can use six iteration recipes to make new versions of a winner.
You can spot fatigue with numbers and set a refresh cadence for your budget.

steps.h: A winner is a starting point
steps.p: A winning concept is not the end of testing; it is the best place to keep testing. Iterations of a proven idea succeed more often than brand new concepts, and they keep the winner fresh when it starts to tire. Losers, meanwhile, must stop quickly so their budget can fund the next idea.

steps.p: These are starting rules to adapt, the same lines used throughout the school. Write them in your log before launch and apply them without debate. Judge on network data after the lag check.

steps.say: These are the exact starting rules, the same lines used across the school. Zero conversions at two times target spend: kill. C P A, cost per acquisition, over one point five times target after three times spend: kill. Between zero point eight and one point five: hold and add iterations. Zero point eight or less with three plus conversions: confirm, iterate, and scale by twenty percent. A winner over one point two times its own average three days in a row: fatigue check. And an iteration twenty percent cheaper that passes the gap rule becomes the new control.

steps.p: Each recipe keeps the winning angle and core message and changes one surface element. Start at the top: the cheapest change that might restore attention. Module 3 called this the iteration ladder; here are the recipes in detail.
d: Hook swap|same body, three new openings
First frame|new opening image or thumbnail
New real creator|same script, a different person with consent
Length cut|a 15-second cut of a 30-second winner
Format port|video to static or carousel
steps.say: Here are six iteration recipes. Each keeps the winning angle and message, and changes one surface element. Hook swap: same body, three new openings. First frame: a new opening image or thumbnail. New real creator: same script, a different person, with consent. Length cut: a fifteen-second cut of a thirty-second winner. Format port: video to static or carousel. And localise: language, currency and payment method. Start at the top, with the cheapest change that might restore attention.

steps.h: A hook-swap round, step by step
steps.p: The hook swap is the most used recipe because it is cheap and often moves results. Keep the winning body untouched, so any change in results comes from the opening.
d: Write 3 hooks on the same angle
steps.say: The hook swap is the most used recipe, because it's cheap and often moves results. Follow the flow. Keep the winning body untouched. Write three hooks on the same angle. Produce three cuts. Launch them beside the control. And read at three times target spend. Because the body stays the same, any change in results comes from the opening.

steps.p: Example: control C7 runs at about $20 per FTD. Three hook swaps are tested beside it at $75 each, target $25, FTDs from network data, 5 days. Apply the rules, then the gap rule against the control.

Down 25% or more from its best week

steps.p: Bigger budgets reach the same people faster, so they need new ads more often. Use these as starting rules and adjust them to how fast your own winners tire in your geo.
d: Under $50 a day|1 to 2 iterations every 2 weeks
$50 to $200 a day|2 to 3 iterations and 1 concept weekly
Over $200 a day|5 or more new ads weekly
Any budget|never rely on a single ad

Treat these as starting rules, and adjust them to how fast your own winners tire.

steps.p: How you kill matters as much as when. Most damage comes from pausing a winner with nothing ready, or from deleting ads and losing their history.

a.title: Killing badly
items: Keep a loser because it looks nice

b.title: Killing well
items: Add iterations, pause once one carries volume
Kill only at a written line
Log why it lost and what to try next

On the right, killing well: add iterations, and pause the winner once one carries the volume. Pause, never delete. Kill only at a written line. And log why it lost and what to try next.

steps.p: Buyers who test in bursts run out of winners and panic. Buyers who test every week always have something new coming. A weekly sprint makes testing a habit with a fixed budget, a fixed day for decisions and a log that grows every week.

steps.p: Every week runs the same five steps. The read and iterate steps of this week feed the brief of next week, so the loop gets smarter as your log grows.

exam.q: Test budget $240, target cost per FTD $20. Using the concept count formula and range rule, how many concepts should you test?
exam.why: 3 × $20 = $60 per concept, and $240 ÷ $60 = 4, inside the 3 to 6 range.

exam.q: You spent $45 on a concept, 0 FTDs on network data, target $20, postback confirmed working. What do you do?
options: Change the hook and keep the data
Kill it and log the reason
exam.why: 2x target is $40. At $45 with zero FTDs and working tracking, the kill rule fires.

exam.q: Your new concept costs $11 per registration against a $6 target. A teammate suggests five hook tests on it. Best reply?
options: Go back to testing new concepts
exam.why: ($11 − $6) ÷ $11 is about 45%. Hook tests on a weak concept rarely close a gap that big; climb back to concepts.

exam.q: Five concepts share one ad set. After $100, concept E spent $4 against a $25 target. How should E be logged?
options: Unproven; re-test alone if early signals were fine
exam.why: E spent 0.16x target. Under 1x target spend, an ad is unproven because of delivery bias, not proven bad.

exam.q: Ad A: 1,200 impressions, CTR 2.2%. Ad B: 1,300 impressions, CTR 0.9%. Target $25 per FTD; each has spent $6. What now?
options: Wait for more impressions before acting
exam.why: Neither has 2,000 impressions or $12.50 spend (0.5x target), so it is too early to read CTR or act on it.

exam.q: After 3x target spend: Concept X $22 per FTD (6 FTDs), Concept Y $24 (5 FTDs), target $25. Which call is right?
exam.why: $22 is 0.88x and $24 is 0.96x target, both in the hold band. The gap is about 8%, so neither is a clear winner.

exam.q: Platform shows 28 registrations for an ad, the network 26 registrations and 4 FTDs. Spend $75, target $25. Your call?
options: Confirm in a fresh ad set, then scale in 20% steps
exam.why: Tracking agrees (within about 20%). $75 ÷ 4 = $18.75 = 0.75x target with 4 FTDs, which passes the scale line after confirmation.

exam.q: A winner averaged $20 per FTD. Last 3 days: $23, $25, $26. CTR fell from 1.5% to 1.2%. What is the best action?
options: Add 2 to 3 iterations beside it now and keep watching
exam.why: CPA is over 1.2 × $20 = $24 on two of three days only, and CTR fell 20%, under the 25% line. Prepare a refresh by adding iterations; do not pause a still-profitable winner.

exam.q: A teammate wants to test an ad showing an actor saying 'I made $500 in my first week'. What do you say?
options: Run it only in a small test
exam.why: An actor posing as a customer with an income claim misleads people and breaks platform rules. No test budget makes it acceptable.

exam.q: You spend $30 a day and have one winner. How often should you add new creatives under the starting cadence?
exam.why: Under $50 a day, plan 1 to 2 iterations every two weeks, and never rely on a single ad.
